Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Communicate clearly and empathetically with patients and their families
Situation2: A patient has received a new diagnosis for a chronic condition and has many questions about managing it.
Story: My phone buzzed insistently at 2 a.m., jolting me from a shallow sleep. It was Sam, my closest friend, his voice trembling as he choked out the news of his father’s sudden passing. I could hear the raw pain in his words, and every instinct as a friend screamed at me to stay on the line, to listen, to be the shoulder he needed right now. But as I tried to comfort him, my hospital pager vibrated—one of my patients, newly diagnosed with diabetes, was awake and anxious, asking for me. I knew she was scared and needed reassurance, clear answers, and a calm presence. My heart twisted as I realized I couldn’t be fully present for both. Sam needed me to listen, to just be there, while my patient needed me to guide her through the confusion and fear. I sat on the edge of my bed, torn, the weight of both expectations pressing down, unsure which call to answer first.
